doc.title: Don Menza and Sam Noto interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, January 28, 1997

title: Rich giving Menza space; the Riverboat story
summary: Rich never limited his solos, and the night at the Riverboat after Menza's daughter was born.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: matter what you did, you could play really well, but everybody’s, “Well it sure wasn’t much like what Don played.”

You know I played it every night and I had a bag of tricks, and the bag kept getting bigger and bigger, and I had all the space in the world. He never told me, hey cut it short. Never once said that, no matter how long or how absurd or bizarre I got with what I played, he said, “You got it, that’s you.” And people said you have to see him on the drums in back of you — he’s got his foot up on the bass drum and he’s listening and looking at me, laughing you know, and like sometimes he’d egg me on — “yeah, that’s it, play, yeah,” he’d be screaming at me you know. And it was great. He gave me all the space in the world, he never once handcuffed me. I’ll tell you one night Joe Romano and I partied all day in New York. My daughter had just been born, this was October of ‘68. And we were working at The Riverboat. And Joe Romano and I walked in and I had a box of Havana cigars and we had been drinking all day. And we walked in and we did look a bit disheveled, you know, and I’m trying not to look at him. And at The Riverboat they had buttons on the floor right where I sat, and I had to press the button to turn the lights on and there was another button to step on to open the curtain. Well I could see him looking at Joe and Joe has this classic look about when he’s been partying too much, his hair down in front of his face. I didn’t have that luxury you know. And Joe is sitting there and he’s like warming up, and Buddy goes over and pulls his locks from his eyes and he says “uh huh,” and then he looks down at me and I’m fooling with my reed and I’m trying not to look at him, and of course with me my eyes are bright red and I’m trying not to look at him and he says, “Uh huh,” and he says, “okay,” he says, “Willowcrest,” which is a tenor-alto feature. And he used to play it fast [humms] in three [humms]. And he’d start playing and he’d scream, “Willowcrest” he says “Menza, get the lights, get the curtains.” Well I reach over and press this thing and all the lights go out, I pressed the wrong button. And then he says, “The lights, the lights!” And the lights are blinking on and off and I can’t get the curtain thing to work, and finally I stand up and I’m trying to find the button, and I’m looking at him and I’m like this, and I press the button, the lights go on, the curtains open, and I’m out in front of the band looking like this, and he cut the band off and he says, “This isn’t your band.” He comes out, closes the curtain, and he got on my case and Joe’s case. He says, “If you guys ever come on my bandstand like this again—” and then he started laughing. He says, “What have you been doing all day?” And the people are waiting for the concert. I said, “My daughter was born last night.” He says, “Oh, congratulations,” he says, “you didn’t bring me anything?” I says, “Yeah, I got you a cigar, I got a bottle of wine, I got a bottle of Cognac.” He says, “Give me these things.” He took the cigar and the bottle of Cognac and the curtain opens and he starts talking to the people about my daughter.
He was nuts man. Buddy was a natural guy. He did what he thought at that minute you know?

And that night is the night where my father-in-law and all my relatives from Long Island were in to The Riverboat to hear us play, and we went up to the bar and they wouldn’t let us stand at the bar. They says, “Uh huh, this isn’t for the band, you guys go down.” I says, “Don’t move.” I says, “Hey Buddy, they won’t let us — my family’s up there.” He says, “Who?” And he’s in the dressing room, slippers, this was after the first set, with a bathrobe, and he had his toupee off, and he says, “Who?” He walks straight through the club, up a big circular staircase that looked like “Gone With the Wind,” he says, “Where?” I says, “That guy over there.” “If you ever mess with my band again,” he says, “we’re out of here.” He says, “Guys, the drinks are on me.”
Oh, man that’s a great story.

Buddy was incredible. Yeah. You hear a lot of bad stories, a lot of people don’t like him. A lot of people, oh, hey, he was too arrogant and everything. He was a pussycat. He really was. And I’ll tell you he is sorely missed. That’s the kind of drummer that helps, he knows about playing the time, he knows about when to get exciting, you know maybe not my favorite way of playing, but I never heard anybody play any better.
